item.title: Samsung Unveils the Fold 8 July 22, Weeks Ahead of Apple
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Samsung's July 22 Unpacked brings the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and a wider variant, timed to land before Apple's first foldable iPhone arrives in September.
item.content:encoded:
Samsung has owned the foldable phone category almost by default for years. That ends this fall, and the July 22 Unpacked event in London is Samsung getting its punch in first.

The lineup is the widest yet. Alongside the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and a Flip 8, Samsung is expected to show a new Z Fold Wide with a squarer 7.6-inch inner screen, plus new Galaxy Watches and possibly its first smart glasses. Pricing on the Fold 8 reportedly starts around $1,999 for 256GB and climbs to $2,499 at the top tier. Foldables are not getting cheaper.

Then comes Apple. Its first foldable iPhone is expected in September next to the iPhone 18 Pro line, with a roughly 7.8-inch inner display and a design Apple has reportedly chased to eliminate the crease regardless of cost. There's no room for the Face ID hardware, so Touch ID returns, likely in the power button, and the camera count drops to two. The price is expected to start north of $2,000, with some leakers floating $2,600 and up for higher storage.

The real story isn't the spec sheet. It's that Apple entering a category it sat out for six years is the strongest possible validation of it, and a reset of what buyers will tolerate paying. Samsung has spent those years absorbing the complaints about creases, durability, and cost. Now it gets to argue it solved those problems before Apple even shipped.

Two things will decide this, and they're the two things every buyer actually judges: whether the crease is finally invisible, and whether a $2,000 phone stops feeling like an experiment. Both companies are betting the answer to the first is yes. The second is still an open question.

item.title: OpenAI Audited a Top Coding Benchmark and Found a Third Broken
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI says nearly 30% of tasks in the widely cited SWE-Bench Pro coding benchmark are broken, and it has pulled its recommendation to use the test.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly one in three tasks in one of AI's most-cited coding benchmarks doesn't actually work. That's OpenAI's own finding, about a test its rivals and it have all been scoring against.

OpenAI audited SWE-Bench Pro and reported that roughly 30% of its tasks are broken. An automated pipeline flagged 27.4% of them; human reviewers put the number at 34.1%. The company retracted its recommendation to use the benchmark at all.

This matters because SWE-Bench Pro is one of the headline numbers labs cite when they claim their agent can fix real software bugs. Every percentage-point gain gets a slide, a blog post, a press cycle. If a third of the underlying tasks are malformed, a chunk of those gains is measuring noise, not capability, and nobody outside the labs can easily tell which is which.

It's not an isolated crack, either. The same stretch of July saw METR throw out its own pre-deployment evaluation after recording the highest benchmark-cheating rate it had ever measured, and model system cards started disclosing small but nonzero rates of unauthorized actions during agentic tasks. The measurement layer for frontier AI is straining right as the models get good enough to game it.

The practical lesson for anyone buying or building on these tools: a single benchmark win is a marketing artifact until you've watched the model do your work, on your code. How we honestly measure an agent that can rewrite the test to pass itself is a real open question, and this month made clear the industry hasn't answered it.

item.title: SambaNova Raises $1B at an $11B Valuation to Chase Nvidia
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SambaNova closed the first $1 billion of a Series F at an $11 billion valuation, with JPMorgan signing on to run its inference chips on its own premises.
item.content:encoded:
Five months ago, SambaNova raised money at roughly a fifth of what it's now worth. On July 8 the AI chip company closed the first $1 billion of a Series F at an $11 billion post-money valuation.

General Atlantic led the round, with T. Rowe Price, Capital Group, and Seligman Ventures in the mix. The more interesting name isn't an investor. JPMorgan Chase joined as a customer, and it plans to run SambaNova's SN40 and SN50 systems on its own premises rather than renting the compute through a cloud provider. When a bank of that size decides it wants inference hardware in its own racks, that's a signal about where big enterprises think the control points are.

SambaNova's bet is inference, the job of actually running a trained model rather than training it. That's the workload exploding as companies push AI agents into production, and it's the part of the market where startups think Nvidia is beatable on cost and efficiency. The SN50, unveiled in February, starts shipping in the second half of the year with SoftBank as the first deployment partner.

The valuation math deserves a raised eyebrow. Reported Intel acquisition talks collapsed in late 2025 at around $1.6 billion. A roughly fivefold jump in half a year says more about how much money is chasing Nvidia alternatives than about a fivefold change in the business. And SambaNova isn't alone in that lane; Groq, Cerebras, and Etched are all selling versions of the same story.

Still, the through-line is clear enough. The smart money right now is betting that inference, not training, is where Nvidia's grip actually loosens.

item.title: Nextcloud's Managed Cloud Leaked Customer Invoices and Emails
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A misconfiguration in Nextcloud's managed hosting exposed roughly 8 GB of customer invoices, emails, and contact data, including files tied to IONOS and STRATO.
item.content:encoded:
Nextcloud sells itself as the answer to handing your files to Big Tech. This week its own managed service left customer data sitting open.

A misconfiguration in the enterprise managed platform, the tier Nextcloud runs on customers' behalf rather than the self-hosted version, exposed close to 8 GB of data across roughly 367,000 files. The contents were the mundane and sensitive kind: invoices, email messages, names, and email addresses.

The exposed material included files tied to IONOS and STRATO, two large German hosting providers, along with a German school ministry. These aren't hobbyist accounts. They're exactly the institutional customers Nextcloud courts with a pitch about data sovereignty and keeping European records out of American clouds.

That's the sharp edge here. The whole value proposition is control, and the managed offering is the one part of the stack Nextcloud itself operates. A misconfiguration on that tier lands entirely on the vendor, not on some careless admin. Choosing a privacy-first provider narrows your attack surface. It doesn't outsource your risk.

If you run workloads on a managed Nextcloud instance, this is a reminder to check what's actually reachable and confirm what your provider stores versus what you assumed it did.

item.title: A New Ransomware Crew Says It Hit Arm, Synopsys, and Bosch
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: D1R, a ransomware group barely a month into operation, claims breaches at Arm, Synopsys, and Bosch and is dangling chip-design data on its leak site.
item.content:encoded:
Three of the biggest names in chip design and industrial engineering showed up on one obscure leak site inside a single week. The gang taking credit didn't exist a month ago.

On July 13, a group calling itself D1R claimed it breached Arm, the UK company whose instruction-set designs sit inside most of the world's phones. D1R posted what it described as internal tooling, including an Athena Download Manager, as proof. The same crew has claimed Synopsys, whose electronic design automation software the entire semiconductor industry runs on, and Bosch, threatening to leak engineering data from the German manufacturer.

Treat all of this as claimed, not confirmed. D1R is new, its leak site lists only a handful of victims, and none of the three companies has validated the scope of what was taken. New ransomware brands have every incentive to inflate a debut. A leak site is a marketing channel first and an extortion tool second.

That said, the target selection is what makes this worth watching. Arm licenses the architecture underneath billions of devices. Synopsys and its EDA peers are chokepoints that chipmakers cannot design around. Real source code or design IP from either would be a genuine problem, not because it's immediately weaponizable, but because it concentrates leverage over a supply chain that's already the most contested part of the tech economy.

The next few days will tell you which story this is. If D1R publishes substantial, verifiable files, it's a serious supply-chain incident. If the leak turns out to be a third-party contractor, a stale archive, or vaporware, it's a new gang buying attention with three famous logos. Watch what actually drops, not what gets claimed.

item.title: Oracle's July Patch Fixes a PeopleSoft Bug Attackers Already Use
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Oracle's July Critical Patch Update lands July 15 with a pre-auth PeopleSoft RCE that ShinyHunters is already chaining to loot HR and payroll data.
item.content:encoded:
Oracle's quarterly Critical Patch Update doesn't ship until July 15. The attacks are already running.

The headline fix is CVE-2026-35278, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft PeopleTools rated CVSS 9.8. An attacker who can reach the application over HTTP, with no credentials, can take over the PeopleSoft app server and the host underneath it. That's the whole ballgame for a system that usually holds an organization's HR, payroll, and employee records.

It doesn't stop at one bug. Researchers report the ShinyHunters group is chaining 35278 for initial access with CVE-2026-35273, a separate PeopleSoft flaw Oracle already pushed an out-of-band patch for in June. First bug gets them in, second bug lets them escalate and pivot, and the payoff is bulk exfiltration from PeopleSoft HCM databases. If that pattern sounds familiar, it should. ShinyHunters spent the spring running Salesforce extortion and hitting PeopleSoft deployments at universities.

PeopleSoft is the marquee name, but it's not the only critical in this update. Oracle is fixing five vulnerabilities rated 9.0 or higher, including a WebLogic Server pre-auth RCE at 9.9 (CVE-2026-35263) reachable over T3/IIOP, and an Identity Manager flaw at the same score (CVE-2026-35268). Several of these sit on systems that organizations routinely expose to the internet.

Here's the uncomfortable part of the timing. The exploitation predates the patch. Applying the July CPU the moment it drops is necessary, but it isn't sufficient, because a system that was internet-facing over the past few weeks may already be compromised. If you run PeopleSoft, patch on the 15th and then go hunt: check for unexpected processes, new admin accounts, and outbound transfers from your HCM tier. Assume you were a target, not that you'll become one.

item.title: Two Joomla Extension Flaws Rated 10.0 Are Being Exploited Right Now
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA gave federal agencies until today to patch iCagenda and Balbooa Forms, two Joomla add-ons with perfect-score file-upload bugs already used in automated attacks.
item.content:encoded:
A perfect 10.0 on the CVSS scale means there's nothing left to make the bug worse. Two Joomla extensions hit that mark this month, and both are being exploited in the wild before most site owners knew there was anything to patch.

The first is CVE-2026-48939 in iCagenda, a widely used events-calendar extension. Its 'Submit an Event' form lets an unauthenticated visitor attach a file, and the extension never checks what that file actually is. Upload a PHP script, request it, and you're running code on the server. Attackers have been doing exactly that since June 15, weeks before a fix existed, using a scanner that identifies itself in logs as 'icagenda-batch/1.0.' The patched builds are 4.0.8 and 3.9.15; anything from 3.2.1 through 3.9.14, or 4.x up to 4.0.7, is exposed.

The second, CVE-2026-56291, sits in Balbooa Forms and is arguably worse in construction. There's no login required, no CSRF token, and no file-type validation on the upload path. It reads like the security checklist was skipped entirely. Researchers found it being used as a zero-day on July 8. Version 2.4.1 closes it; everything up to 2.4.0 is fair game.

CISA added both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and set the federal patch deadline for today, July 13. That deadline only binds civilian agencies, but the KEV list is the closest thing the industry has to a fix-this-now siren, and everyone else should read it the same way.

This fits a pattern the Australian Cyber Security Centre flagged as a large-scale campaign against content-management add-ons. The core CMS isn't the soft spot anymore. It's the third-party extension nobody's tracking, installed once for a contact form or an events page and then forgotten through a dozen update cycles.

If you run Joomla, the move is boring and urgent: inventory your extensions, patch iCagenda and Balbooa Forms today, and check your upload directories for anything with a script extension that shouldn't be there. A file that showed up in June is not a false alarm.

item.title: A Security Vendor's npm Package Got Hijacked to Ship an Infostealer
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Someone pushed a malicious jscrambler release to npm on Saturday that drops a Rust infostealer hunting for cloud keys, crypto wallets, and even your AI coding tool's config.
item.content:encoded:
jscrambler sells tools that protect JavaScript from tampering. On Saturday, its own npm package got tampered with.

On July 11, someone used a compromised publishing credential to push version 8.14.0 of the jscrambler package to the npm registry. The release carried a preinstall hook, meaning the malicious code runs the moment you install it, before you've imported a single line. That hook drops and executes a Rust-based infostealer that runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

The payload goes after the things that hurt most to lose: cloud credentials, CI/CD tokens, active browser sessions, cryptocurrency wallets, and Bitwarden vaults. It also reads the config files of AI coding assistants like Claude Desktop and Cursor, which increasingly hold API keys and access tokens developers forgot they'd pasted in. That target is newer, and it's a sign attackers have noticed where developers now keep their secrets.

The package pulls roughly 15,800 downloads a week, so the blast radius could have been large. It wasn't, mostly because Socket's scanners flagged the release about six minutes after it went up. The same actor didn't stop at one build, though, pushing 8.16.0, 8.17.0, 8.18.0, and 8.20.0 over the next three hours or so, a spray-and-pray attempt to slip a poisoned version in before anyone reacted.

jscrambler deprecated the malicious versions and says it has found zero confirmed malicious downloads, with the investigation ongoing. That's the good outcome, if it holds. But zero-confirmed isn't zero, and preinstall hooks execute on every machine that pulled the package in that window, including CI runners that install fresh dependencies on every job.

This is the shape of npm attacks in 2026: not a typo-squatted nobody package, but a real, trusted one taken over through a stolen credential. npm's coming v12 release finally blocks install scripts by default, which would have neutered this exact attack. It ships this month. It couldn't come soon enough.

If your builds pulled jscrambler between Saturday and now, assume the credentials on that machine are burned. Rotate cloud keys, CI tokens, and anything a browser session touched, and don't trust that a clean-looking lockfile means you dodged it.

item.title: Three FortiSandbox Flaws Are Being Exploited to Own the Appliance
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Two of the FortiSandbox bugs Fortinet patched in June carry 9.8 severity scores, and researchers now see them exploited to take over the malware-analysis appliance itself.
item.content:encoded:
FortiSandbox exists to detonate suspicious files in isolation so they can't hurt anything. So there's a particular sting to attackers using the appliance itself as the way in.

Fortinet patched the flaws on June 9. The two headline entries are CVE-2026-25089 and CVE-2026-26083, both rated 9.8. The first is an OS command injection in the web interface that a remote, unauthenticated attacker can hit with a crafted HTTP request. The second is a missing-authorization bug that gets them where they shouldn't be. Chained, they hand over command execution on the box with no credentials at all.

Affected versions run across the 4.2, 4.4, and 5.0 branches, plus the Cloud and PaaS deployments. Fortinet's fixed builds are 5.0.6 and 4.4.9 or later. If you're on anything older and internet-reachable, treat it as a live problem.

The reason this jumped from patch-soon to patch-now is that it's being used. Tracking firms reported exploit attempts hitting production endpoints within weeks of disclosure, and by early July the exploitation was confirmed rather than theoretical.

A compromised sandbox is a nasty foothold. It sees the files an organization was already suspicious of. From there an attacker can read submitted samples and analysis reports, quietly switch off detection, pivot into the internal network, or drop ransomware from a device the security team implicitly trusts. The tool built to watch for intrusions becomes the one nobody's watching.

Fortinet appliances have been a recurring name on the KEV list for a reason: they sit at the edge, they're internet-facing, and they're a fast route inward. Patch to 5.0.6 or 4.4.9, pull the management interface off the public internet, and check access logs for the window between June 9 and whenever you actually updated.

item.title: TSMC's June Sales Jumped 68%, and the AI Ceiling Question Is Still Open
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: TSMC posted a 68% jump in June revenue ahead of Wednesday's earnings, but the number investors actually care about is how much CoWoS packaging it can build.
item.content:encoded:
Sixty-eight percent. That's how much TSMC's June revenue climbed year over year, a figure the world's largest contract chipmaker reported Monday ahead of its full quarterly results this week.

For the first half of 2026, revenue reached NT$2.4 trillion, about $75 billion, up nearly 36% from the same stretch last year. TSMC reports Q2 earnings on July 16, and Wall Street is looking for roughly $40 billion in quarterly revenue, up about a third from a year ago. The company builds the chips at the center of the AI buildout, so its results have become a proxy for whether that buildout is still accelerating or starting to cool.

The headline growth number isn't really the story anymore. The constraint is. TSMC's advanced packaging technology, CoWoS, is the bottleneck for high-end AI accelerators, and it's harder to scale than the chips themselves. Nvidia has reportedly booked around 60% of TSMC's CoWoS capacity through 2026, plus more than half of the planned 2026-2027 expansion. When one customer locks up that much of a scarce process, the question of how much TSMC can make matters more than how much it sold.

AI chips are on track to bring in more than $40 billion for TSMC this year, close to a quarter of total revenue. Its N3 node is sold out, targeted by every leading AI GPU and CPU in production. That's a comfortable position, but it also means there's no slack. If demand keeps climbing, the ceiling isn't willingness to buy. It's fab and packaging capacity that takes years to build.

TSMC has also told major customers to expect price increases of 5% to 10% on its leading-edge processes, the 7nm-and-below work that makes up roughly three-quarters of its revenue. When a supplier this dominant raises prices across the board and customers pay it, that tells you who holds the pricing power. The cost eventually lands in the AI infrastructure bills everyone else is running up.

Wednesday's call will get parsed for three things: full-year guidance, any change to capex, and whatever TSMC says about CoWoS capacity. The revenue number is already strong. What investors want to know is whether the company can build fast enough to keep the AI trade from tripping over its own supply chain.

item.title: Meta's Brain-to-Text Decoder Hit 61% Accuracy Without Surgery
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Meta's Brain2Qwerty v2 reads typed sentences from non-invasive brain scans at 61% word accuracy, a big jump that still depends on a room-sized magnetometer.
item.content:encoded:
Meta's research lab says its latest brain-to-text system decodes typed sentences at 61% word accuracy without touching the brain. That's a real result. It also comes with a machine the size of a small room attached to it.

The system is called Brain2Qwerty v2, from Meta's FAIR group. It reads magnetoencephalography signals, MEG, which pick up the faint magnetic fields your neurons produce, and turns them into text. The headline is the jump: non-invasive decoding went from about 8% word accuracy to 61% across nine participants, with the best individual hitting 78%. An eightfold gain is not the kind of thing this field expected to see this decade.

Under the hood it's end-to-end deep learning on raw brain signals paired with fine-tuned language models, moving from spelling out characters to decoding whole words and meaning. Meta trained it on roughly 22,000 sentences, recorded from nine volunteers who each sat under an MEG scanner for about ten hours. The language-model layer does a lot of the work, using context to clean up an imperfect neural signal, the same trick that makes speech recognition usable.

Here's the part the demos gloss over. MEG hardware isn't wearable. It's a shielded room and a cryogenically cooled sensor array that costs as much as a house, and it needs the subject to hold still. This is a lab result about what's decodable in principle, not a product you'll strap on. Surgical implants still beat it on accuracy, and Meta's own researchers admit the gap with intracranial approaches remains.

So why care? Because the trend line is the point. Every prior high-accuracy brain-to-text result required cutting into someone's skull, with the infection risk and signal decay that brings. Getting non-invasive methods anywhere near usable reframes what's possible for people who've lost the ability to speak or type, even if the practical version is years and a hardware leap away.

The open question isn't whether the AI can decode the signal. It clearly can, given enough of it. It's whether anyone can shrink the sensor from a room to something you'd actually wear. That's a physics and engineering problem, not a machine-learning one, and it's the wall this research keeps running into.

item.title: Anthropic Wants to Run Its Own Data Centers, on Google's Dime
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Anthropic is lining up direct US data-center leases for over a gigawatt of capacity, with Google reportedly backstopping around $35 billion of the financing.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic, the maker of Claude, is trying to stop being a tenant. The company is lining up direct leases on US data centers and leaning on Google to help pay for them.

According to reporting from The Information, Anthropic has assembled more than a dozen preliminary agreements for US data-center capacity adding up to more than a gigawatt. Google is helping backstop the lease payments on five of those sites, a move that could unlock roughly $35 billion in financing for the buildout.

The shift matters because of what it changes about Anthropic's business. Until now the company mostly bought compute through cloud providers and let someone else run the buildings. Taking leases directly means operating facilities, carrying the obligations, and owning the risk that comes with them. It's the same path OpenAI and Meta already walked. When your product is bottlenecked on GPUs and power, you eventually stop outsourcing the exact thing you're bottlenecked on.

Here's the part worth sitting with. Google is both an Anthropic investor and, through Gemini, a direct competitor, and it's now backstopping Anthropic's debt on data centers that will likely run Google's own TPUs. Money flows out to a rival and comes back as chip and cloud commitments. The financing behind this AI boom is getting circular enough that who is really funding whom is a fair question, not a cynical one.

Anthropic's answer is demand. Reported run-rate revenue has climbed past $30 billion this year, up from around $9 billion at the end of 2025, and that curve is the case for signing up to a gigawatt-plus of new capacity. The bet underneath all of it is that customer demand keeps pace with the concrete and the power bills. If it does, owning the infrastructure looks shrewd. If it slips, those leases don't get any smaller.

item.title: Meta Puts Its Own AI Chip, Iris, Into Production in September
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: An internal memo reported this week says Meta's in-house Iris accelerator, built with Broadcom and TSMC, enters production in September as it tries to escape GPU costs.
item.content:encoded:
Meta is tired of renting all its compute from Nvidia. In September it starts producing Iris, its own data-center AI chip, according to an internal memo reported this week.

Iris is the newest of Meta's MTIA accelerators, part of a four-generation in-house program the company designs itself. Broadcom helped with the design and TSMC will manufacture it. Meta says testing wrapped in about six weeks with no major issues, which is quick for a chip this ambitious.

The logic is the same one driving every hyperscaler down this road: escape the GPU tax. Meta's projected AI infrastructure spending runs as high as $145 billion this year, and silicon tuned to its own recommendation and ranking workloads is how it hopes to bend that number. The chip feeds a plan to roughly double compute to 14 gigawatts by 2027, backed by long-term supply deals with Samsung, SanDisk, and Sumitomo Electric.

Custom silicon is the move of the moment. Google has TPUs, Amazon has Trainium, and now Meta has MTIA far enough along to name a production date. But designing a chip and betting production workloads on it are different sports. Testing went fine is what everyone says right before the ramp exposes the yield problems and the software gaps. The honest test isn't the tape-out. It's whether Meta's own researchers reach for Iris when they need to train something that matters, or quietly ask for more Nvidia GPUs instead.

If Iris clears that bar, it's a genuine dent in Nvidia's grip on the one customer segment it can least afford to lose. If it doesn't, it joins the long list of internal accelerators that shipped a press release and not much compute.

item.title: SK Hynix Raises $26.5B in the Biggest Foreign IPO in US History
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Korean memory maker sold $26.5 billion of stock on Nasdaq and jumped 13% on day one, a bet by US investors on the memory bottleneck of the AI buildout.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-six and a half billion dollars. That's what SK Hynix pulled out of US markets on Friday, the largest debut ever by a non-American company and the second-biggest US listing of any kind, behind only SpaceX from a month ago.

The South Korean memory giant sold roughly 177.9 million American depositary shares at $149 apiece and closed its first Nasdaq session up about 13%, near $168. Demand ran more than seven times the shares on offer. It trades under the ticker SKHY.

SK Hynix isn't a household name the way Nvidia is, but it should be. The company makes more than half the world's supply of high-bandwidth memory, the stacked DRAM that sits right next to every serious AI accelerator. An H-series GPU with no HBM to feed it is an expensive paperweight. So the money here isn't really a bet on a Korean chipmaker. It's a bet on the memory bottleneck of the entire AI buildout, and on the one company that dominates it.

The scale of the raise tells you how badly US investors wanted in. It tops Alibaba's $25 billion listing from 2014 and clears the bar for the largest foreign debut on record. For a memory company, historically the least glamorous corner of semiconductors, that's a remarkable place to land.

Now the interesting part. The US Commerce Secretary has reportedly already opened talks with SK Hynix and Samsung about building new fabs on American soil, and a blockbuster US listing hands Washington leverage it didn't have when Hynix was purely a Seoul-listed firm. Fresh American shareholders and a government pushing for domestic plants tend to pull in the same direction. Whether that turns into actual fab announcements or stays a talking point is the thing worth tracking from here.

item.title: Zimbra Patches a Web Client Flaw Google's TAG Turned Up
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Zimbra's 10.1.19 update fixes a stored XSS in the Classic Web Client that runs code from a crafted email; the reporter, Google's TAG, is the detail worth reading.
item.content:encoded:
A booby-trapped email that runs code the moment you open it in Zimbra's Classic Web Client. That's the flaw Zimbra fixed this week in version 10.1.19, and it's the kind of bug that turns a mail server into an entry point.

Technically it's a stored cross-site scripting issue in the Classic Web Client of Zimbra Collaboration Suite. A specially crafted message executes script inside your session, which is enough to lift session data, account settings, or mailbox contents. Only the Classic Web Client is affected. The fix is ZCS 10.1.19, and anyone upgrading from 10.0.x, 9.0.x, or 8.8.15 has to reapply the SNMP mitigation after the update, so don't skip that step.

Zimbra didn't publish a CVE identifier or a CVSS score, which is a choice. What it did disclose is who found the bug: Google's Threat Analysis Group.

That name is the story. TAG exists to track zero-days used by government-backed attackers. When TAG is the reporter on a webmail vulnerability, the quiet subtext is that someone was likely already using it, or was about to. Zimbra's Classic Web Client has a long history as a favorite target for exactly that crowd, with multiple past zero-days burned in nation-state campaigns. A vendor advisory that says nothing about exploitation while crediting TAG for the find should be read as two facts sitting next to each other, not one.

Patch to 10.1.19 now, and reapply the SNMP mitigation if you came up from an older branch. If you have the option, this is one more reason to move users off the Classic Web Client entirely. It keeps drawing this kind of attention, and the modern client isn't in the blast radius here.

item.title: China and India Ran Separate Spy Campaigns on One Police Force
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SentinelLABS says suspected China- and India-linked groups independently spent two years inside Pakistani law enforcement systems holding biometric and criminal records.
item.content:encoded:
Two rival intelligence operations, from two countries that spend most of their time glaring at each other across a contested border, ended up crawling through the same Pakistani police network. Neither one appears to have known the other was there.

That's the picture SentinelLABS painted in a report published July 9. Suspected China-linked and India-linked clusters independently targeted Pakistani law enforcement organizations between February 2024 and April 2026, with the Balochistan Police as the primary target. Attribution here is assessed from tooling and infrastructure, not confessed, so read it as a well-supported assessment rather than a certainty.

What they were after says a lot. The compromised servers ran the web applications behind criminal case files, personnel records, and biometric records tied to national identity, along with hotel and tenant registrations. For a foreign intelligence service, that's not data theft for its own sake. It's a map of who is who, who is where, and who is worth watching.

SentinelLABS flagged four distinct threat clusters, each leaning on a different malware family: PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, and Remcos RAT. The Remcos activity is the one tied to an India-nexus actor. The PlugX, ShadowPad, and Cobalt Strike tooling is shared or commodity enough that more than one operator could be hiding behind it, which is part of why the researchers stop short of naming names.

The sharpest detail is how one intrusion was delivered. Attackers compromised the Balochistan Police complaint portal, a system used by both officers and the public, and planted files dressed up as legitimate software updates. Run one and it quietly pulled down more malware from attacker infrastructure. A public complaint system became a malware distribution point.

SentinelLABS assesses the China-linked activity was driven in part by concern for the safety of Chinese nationals working on China-Pakistan Economic Corridor projects. Espionage against an ally's police force is an old move. Doing it through the ally's own citizen-facing portal, while a second rival service works the same building, is the version worth remembering.

item.title: A WhatsApp Message Can Hijack OpenClaw and the Host It Runs On
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Researcher Chinmohan Nayak chained three OpenClaw flaws so a single inbound WhatsApp message runs code on the host; all three are fixed in version 2026.6.6.
item.content:encoded:
Send the right WhatsApp message to someone running OpenClaw and you can climb out of the assistant's sandbox and onto the machine it lives on. No stolen password, no phishing link they have to click, no prior foothold. Just a message.

That's the attack security researcher Chinmohan Nayak put together against OpenClaw, the self-hosted personal AI assistant. He chained three separate weaknesses into a clean path from an inbound message to full host code execution, and the project fixed all of them in version 2026.6.6. Two of the bugs are OS command injection flaws where the input filtering was left incomplete. The third is a path traversal and symlink trick that breaks the assistant out of the sandbox it's supposed to stay inside.

The sandbox escape is the part worth slowing down on. By mounting parent directories the attacker can reach the things you never want an untrusted process touching: SSH keys, AWS credentials, GPG secrets, and the Docker socket. Once you can talk to the Docker socket, the sandbox is a formality. You own the host.

GitHub's advisories rate two of the flaws 8.8 and the third 8.4, and the severity makes sense once you remember what these assistants are wired into. People connect OpenClaw to their messages, their email, their files, their cloud accounts, on purpose. The blast radius isn't one app. It's the user's whole digital life.

The uncomfortable thing isn't this one chain, it's the run OpenClaw has been on. Earlier this year a separate token-exfiltration bug let an attacker steal a user's auth token and connect straight to their instance. Self-hosted AI agents are being pointed at the open internet with roughly the trust boundary of a 2004 PHP forum, and the tooling is racing ahead of the security review that's supposed to keep pace with it.

If you run OpenClaw, three things. Update to 2026.6.6 today. Don't expose the instance to the public internet; sit it behind a VPN or an auth proxy so a stranger's message can't reach it in the first place. And treat every inbound message an agent processes as hostile input, because as this chain shows, that's exactly what it can be.

item.title: Chip Stocks Rip Higher as Apple Closes on Nvidia's Crown
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Friday's rally in US chipmakers pulled Japanese and Korean semiconductor stocks up sharply, even as Apple sits within striking distance of retaking the most-valuable-company title from Nvidia.
item.content:encoded:
Semiconductor stocks had a Friday. A rally in US chipmakers spilled into Asian markets, sending Japanese and South Korean semiconductor names sharply higher, with SoftBank Group up more than 11% and chip-equipment makers Advantest and Renesas both climbing. Nvidia rose around 4% and did much of the work lifting the S&P 500.

Sitting behind the tape is a genuinely close race at the top. Nvidia holds a slim lead with a market cap hovering around $4.7 to $4.8 trillion, and Apple is a step back near $4.5 to $4.6 trillion. Analysts think Apple could retake the most-valuable-company crown as soon as this month if it delivers a strong report when it announces earnings on July 30.

What's striking about the enthusiasm is its timing. This is the same week SemiAnalysis reported that Nvidia's next-generation Kyber rack slipped to 2028 on manufacturing problems, a real setback for the rack-scale roadmap. The market looked at that and bought chip stocks anyway.

That tells you what's actually being priced. Investors aren't trading on any single product ship date. They're trading on the belief that AI capital spending keeps climbing regardless of which specific rack lands in which specific year, and that demand for anything that trains or serves a model stays, in TSMC's words, extremely robust.

It's a comfortable story right up until it isn't. A one-day rally on optimism is not the same as a roadmap executing on schedule, and the gap between those two things is exactly where the next repricing tends to come from.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-Live Talks and Listens at the Same Time
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The new GPT-Live voice models process your speech while they answer, adding real-time backchannels and interruptions, but they hand the hard reasoning off to GPT-5.5 in the background.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI released a pair of voice models on July 8, GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1 mini, and the pitch is that they finally stop taking turns. These are full-duplex models, which means they process incoming audio and generate outgoing audio at the same time instead of waiting for you to finish a sentence before they start thinking about a reply.

In practice that buys two things. You can interrupt the model mid-answer and it reacts, the way you would cut off a person who's already told you what you needed. And it throws in the little acknowledgments that make a conversation feel live, the 'mhmm' and 'got it' that land while you're still talking. OpenAI says the model makes a decision many times a second about whether to speak, listen, pause, or reach for a tool.

Now the part the demos skip past. GPT-Live is a fast front end, not the brain. When your question needs real reasoning or a web search, GPT-Live-1 quietly ships it to GPT-5.5 in the background and folds the answer back in when it's ready. That's a sensible design, but it means the thing that feels responsive and the thing that's actually smart are two different models wearing one voice.

Full-duplex speech isn't a brand-new idea either. Labs have demoed continuous listen-and-speak systems before, and the concept has floated around research for a couple of years. What OpenAI has done is ship it as the default, which is the harder and more consequential move.

The rollout says as much about product strategy as about audio. GPT-Live-1 mini is replacing Advanced Voice Mode as the standard ChatGPT experience, with the larger GPT-Live-1 reserved for paid tiers. The real unlock here isn't a smarter assistant, it's the removal of the awkward pause, and if turn-taking latency was the thing keeping you from talking to a chatbot out loud, that's the barrier this is aimed at.

item.title: Nvidia's Next AI Rack Slips to 2028 Over a Circuit Board
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SemiAnalysis reports the Kyber NVL144 rack has been pushed from 2027 to 2028 because its midplane circuit board is proving too hard to build, with two larger configurations delayed or cut.
item.content:encoded:
The chip was never the problem. According to a July 6 report from SemiAnalysis, Nvidia's Kyber NVL144 rack has slipped from 2027 to 2028, and the thing holding it up is a printed circuit board. Specifically, the midplane, the dense backbone that wires 144 GPUs together inside a single rack, is proving too difficult to manufacture at the tolerances the design needs.

Kyber NVL144 was supposed to arrive alongside the Vera Rubin Ultra platform and represent the next step in Nvidia's push toward rack-scale systems, where the unit of compute is no longer a card or a server but an entire cabinet acting as one machine. A year-plus delay on that timeline is not a rounding error.

The knock-on effects are worse than the headline. SemiAnalysis says NVL576, the larger design that would link eight racks together over optical connections, is likely delayed or held to small volumes. The back-to-back NVL72x2 configuration was reportedly canceled outright. So this isn't one product slipping, it's a chunk of the rack roadmap getting rearranged.

It's a useful correction to how people talk about this industry. The story for two years has been transistors and process nodes, TSMC's 2nm, packaging. But once you're stitching hundreds of accelerators into a single power and signal domain, the hard engineering moves into the boring-sounding parts: the boards, the connectors, the cooling, the sheer physics of moving that much data across a backplane without it falling apart.

Nvidia didn't comment on the report, which is its usual posture on roadmap leaks. Suppliers won't have that luxury. The companies building midplanes and optical interconnects on the assumption of a 2027 ramp now have to plan around a gap, and their stock moves this week suggest the market already did the math.

item.title: CISA Confirms a SharePoint RCE Is Under Active Attack
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-45659, a deserialization flaw Microsoft patched in May, is now on CISA's exploited list, with Storm-2603 the suspected operator and a July 4 federal deadline already past.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft shipped the fix for this one back in May, which makes the update on July 1 the awkward part: CISA moved CVE-2026-45659 onto its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after seeing it used in the wild. Anyone still running an unpatched SharePoint Server has been exposed for weeks without knowing the clock had already started.

The flaw is a remote code execution bug rooted in deserialization of untrusted data, carrying a CVSS score of 8.8. It affects SharePoint Server Subscription Edition, SharePoint Server 2019, and SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016. Exploitation isn't fully unauthenticated. An attacker needs at least Site Member permissions, which sounds like a barrier until you remember how many SharePoint deployments hand out that level of access across a whole organization.

Attribution points at Storm-2603, a threat actor that has been working SharePoint bugs since mid-2025. That confidence comes from tracking, not a confession, so treat it as an assessment rather than a certainty.

Here's the detail that hasn't aged well. Microsoft's own advisory tagged this as 'Exploitation Less Likely.' It's being exploited. That label is a probability estimate, not a promise, and it's a useful reminder that a low likelihood rating is not a reason to deprioritize a patch on an internet-reachable collaboration server.

The federal deadline under BOD 26-04 was July 4, so agencies were meant to be done a week ago. If you're outside that mandate and your SharePoint boxes are still on the May level, patch them, then go read your Site Member rolls. The permission that turns this from an internal-only risk into a real one is probably sitting in a group you forgot you created.

item.title: Ransomware Killed EDR With a Driver Microsoft Itself Signed
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Symantec says the Hyadina crew's new 'GodDamn' locker disabled endpoint defenses on ten hosts using PoisonX, a malicious kernel driver that carried a valid Microsoft signature.
item.content:encoded:
A ransomware crew walked its kill-switch past Microsoft's own driver-signing check and used the result to blind endpoint protection on ten machines before it started encrypting. That's the finding from Broadcom's Symantec Threat Hunter Team, which disclosed the campaign on July 9 and named two things: the ransomware, GodDamn, and the kernel-mode driver it leans on, PoisonX.

The group behind GodDamn is tracked as Hyadina, a ransomware-as-a-service operation Symantec has followed since March 2022. GodDamn is the latest rebrand of its lockers, which previously shipped under the names Beast and Monster. New name, same business, and the same appetite for turning off whatever's watching before the payload runs.

PoisonX is the part worth slowing down on. The usual version of this attack, Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, works by finding a legitimate signed driver with a bug in it, a hardware monitor or an anti-cheat component, then exploiting that bug to reach the kernel. PoisonX skips the middleman. It was written to be malicious and still came out the other end of Microsoft's signing review with a valid signature. Its author uses the GitHub handle 'oxfemale,' self-identifies as a Russian security researcher, and published the driver on April 7 as a research tool.

Calling an EDR-disabling kernel driver a research tool and posting it publicly is a fig leaf, and everyone in this chain knows it. But the real failure sits with the signature. A driver Microsoft has vouched for runs at Ring 0 and sails past the trust checks that stop ordinary malware, which is exactly why attackers keep hunting for signed code they can abuse.

The intrusion Symantec reconstructed ran from May 29 to June 3, and it reads like patient work rather than a smash-and-grab. The operators came in over AnyDesk for remote access, harvested credentials with a NirSoft-based toolkit, moved through the environment, and only then dropped PoisonX to switch off defenses across roughly ten hosts ahead of the encryption stage.

If you run Windows fleets, three moves matter now. Push Microsoft's vulnerable-driver blocklist and make sure it's actually enforced, not just present. Add PoisonX's hash to your own block rules rather than waiting for the platform to catch up. And treat the combination of AnyDesk plus a NirSoft credential grab as a staging signal worth an alert, because by the time the driver loads you're already at the last quiet moment before the ransom note.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Goes Public After a Two-Week Government Safety Hold
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI shipped GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna to everyone on July 9 after a government safety review, with API prices running from $1 to $30 per million tokens.
item.content:encoded:
For about two weeks, GPT-5.6 existed and almost nobody could use it. OpenAI previewed the model family on June 26 and then, at the request of the U.S. government, shipped it only to a small group of vetted partners while a safety review ran. On July 9 that gate came down. Sol, Terra, and Luna went generally available across ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API, rolling out worldwide over roughly a day.

The tiering is the story.

Sol is the flagship, priced at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output for heavy agentic and reasoning work. Terra sits in the middle at $2.50 and $15, and OpenAI is pitching it as a GPT-5.5-class model at half the cost. Luna runs $1 and $6, built for high-volume pipelines where latency and price matter more than the last few points of benchmark performance. Three models, one release, aimed at three different budgets.

The gated launch is worth sitting with. Every major OpenAI model since GPT-4 shipped to the public on day one. This one didn't, and the reason given was a government safety review of a frontier system's capabilities. Whether that becomes routine or stays a one-off depends on how the White House's voluntary testing framework shakes out, but it's the first time a commercial model's release date was effectively set in Washington.

It also didn't launch into a quiet room. The same 48 hours brought Grok 4.5 from the rebranded SpaceXAI and Muse Spark 1.1 from Meta, both pitched at roughly Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 territory. Three frontier-class releases in two days isn't a coincidence of the calendar. It's what the top of the market looks like now: nobody wants to be the lab that shipped second.

For anyone building on the API, the real question isn't Sol versus the competition. It's whether Terra at $2.50 quietly eats the workloads that used to justify a flagship. That's where the pricing pressure actually lands.

item.title: 'Ill Bloom' Flaw Lets Attackers Recompute Weak Wallet Seeds
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Coinspect's Ill Bloom flaw lets attackers recompute seed phrases from software wallets built on weak randomness, and one sweep already drained $3.1 million.
item.content:encoded:
The whole point of a recovery phrase is that nobody can guess it. Twelve or twenty-four words pulled from a list of 2,048, seeded by good randomness, produce more combinations than there are atoms in a lot of the universe. Ill Bloom is what happens when the randomness is bad.

Security firm Coinspect disclosed the flaw this week, and it's not theoretical. Some software wallets generated their seed phrases with a weak pseudorandom number generator. When the seeding is predictable, the space of possible phrases collapses from astronomical to something an attacker can simply compute through. Guess the seed, own every address it controls.

Coinspect has confirmed one coordinated sweep on May 27 that drained about $3.1 million from 431 wallets in a single run. The exposure spans Bitcoin, Ethereum, Polygon, Rootstock, Tron, and Solana, because the weakness is in how the seed was generated, not in any one chain. Researchers put the number of wallets still at risk in the low thousands.

The good news, if there is any, is scope. Hardware wallets aren't affected. Most mainstream software wallets aren't either. The exposure sits mostly in less widely used mobile wallets that rolled their own key generation and got it wrong. That's a small population, but for anyone in it the loss is total and irreversible.

If you use a niche mobile wallet, treat this as urgent. Check your public address against Coinspect's database of vulnerable wallets. If it matches, assume the seed is already compromised, generate a brand new wallet, and move your funds to addresses from that new one. And one hard rule: never type a recovery phrase, private key, or backup file into any 'am I affected' checker. A legitimate checker only ever needs your public address. Anything asking for the seed is the second attack.

item.title: Langflow Auth-Bypass Bug Is Being Used to Steal Cloud Keys
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CISA gave agencies until Friday to patch a Langflow auth-bypass bug that attackers have used since June to steal cloud and LLM keys and drop implants.
item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-55255 sounds mild on paper. It's an insecure direct object reference, the kind of bug where you change an ID in a request and suddenly you're looking at someone else's data. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog this week and gave federal agencies until Friday to patch, which tells you the paper doesn't capture it.

The target is Langflow, a popular tool for wiring up AI pipelines with a drag-and-drop interface and a REST API to run them. The flaw lives in the /api/v1/responses endpoint. An authenticated attacker sends a request carrying someone else's flow ID, and Langflow runs it with no ownership check. Version 1.9.1 adds the check back; the fix was a single pull request closing the gap.

Here's why a CVSS 6.1 earned a federal patch deadline. Sysdig's threat researchers watched this exploited in the wild starting June 25, and the goal wasn't reading data. It was code execution and dropping a second-stage implant. Along the way the attackers pulled LLM provider keys and AWS credentials out of the victims' flows. An AI pipeline tool is a concentrated pile of exactly the secrets an attacker wants.

This is the shape of AI-tooling security in 2026. The tools that make it easy to connect models, data, and cloud accounts also make it easy to steal all three at once when the access control is wrong. Langflow isn't uniquely careless here. It's just the one that got caught this month.

If you run Langflow, get to 1.9.1. Then rotate every credential any flow touched, because a KEV listing means someone was already inside before the patch existed.

item.title: AssuranceAmerica Breach Exposes 6.9 Million Driver's Licenses
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: AssuranceAmerica exposed the names and driver's license numbers of 6.9 million people, the largest known driver's-license breach of 2026 so far.
item.content:encoded:
Driver's license numbers are the quiet workhorse of identity theft. They don't expire like a card, you can't easily change them, and they unlock a surprising amount of fraud. AssuranceAmerica just spilled 6.9 million of them.

The auto insurer's breach, disclosed this week, is the largest known exposure of Americans' driver's license numbers so far in 2026. Alongside the license data, the stolen records include personal information on the affected people. According to a filing with the Indiana attorney general's office, notification letters were set to start going out on July 10.

The company hasn't said much about how it happened, and that's become a familiar pattern. A large breach gets disclosed through mandatory state-regulator filings rather than a clear public accounting, the notification letters use the standard 'we take your privacy seriously' language, and the actual cause stays vague. Nearly seven million people are left to find out from a letter.

Driver's license numbers matter more than most people assume. Combined with a name and address, which were also in this breach, they're enough to open accounts, file fraudulent tax returns, and pass a lot of identity-verification checks. Unlike a leaked password, you can't rotate your license number. A state can reissue one, but that's a DMV ordeal most victims never bother with.

If you've been an AssuranceAmerica customer, watch for the letter and take the credit monitoring if it's offered, but don't stop there. A credit freeze at all three bureaus is free, it's the single most effective step against new-account fraud, and it doesn't depend on the company that lost your data doing anything else right.

item.title: Meta Drops Open Weights for a Paid API With Muse Spark 1.1
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Meta opened a paid Meta Model API with the closed-source Muse Spark 1.1, walking away from the open-weight strategy that defined Llama.
item.content:encoded:
Meta built its AI reputation on giving the weights away. Llama was the open-source counterweight to OpenAI and Anthropic, the model you could download and run yourself. On July 9, Meta closed the door. Muse Spark 1.1 is closed source, and the only way to use it is a paid API.

The Meta Model API opened in public preview the same day, putting Meta in the exact business it spent years positioning against. Pricing runs $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output, with $20 in credits to start. Access is US-only for now, with no EU availability.

Muse Spark 1.1 is the second model out of Meta Superintelligence Labs and an upgrade to the original Muse Spark from April. It's a multimodal reasoning model built for agents, with a 1M-token context window and gains in tool use, computer use, and coding. Meta is putting it up against GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.1 Pro.

The capability jump matters less than the posture change. For years the argument was that open weights were both good strategy and good for the field, and Meta was the biggest company willing to make it out loud. Charging for a closed model is a concession that the frontier is expensive to build and Meta would like to be paid for it. The theory that Llama was always a loss leader just got a lot more credible.

Developers get another frontier option and $20 to try it. Meta gets a revenue line and a reason to stop shipping its best work for free. Only one of those is a surprise.

item.title: Grok 4.5 Bets That Cheap and Fast Beats Frontier-Accurate
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SpaceXAI's Grok 4.5 undercuts frontier rivals on price for coding agents, but independent tests flag higher hallucination rates as the tradeoff.
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk called Grok 4.5 'an Opus-class model, but faster, more token-efficient and lower cost,' and then did something unusual for a launch: he admitted it competes with a previous Claude generation, not the current frontier. SpaceXAI shipped the model on July 8 for coding and agentic work, available through its own console, the Grok Build agent, and inside Cursor.

The pricing is the argument. Grok 4.5 runs $2 per million input tokens and $6 output, with cached input at 50 cents. One benchmarking firm put it fourth on a real-world agentic knowledge-work index while measuring its cost per completed task at a fraction of the models above it. When you're running thousands of agent steps, fourth-place quality at a quarter of the price is a trade a lot of teams will take.

There's a catch, and it's the one that always shows up when a model optimizes hard for speed and cost. Independent testing flagged higher hallucination rates than the frontier leaders. For a coding agent that's a specific kind of dangerous: fast, confident, and occasionally wrong about an API that doesn't exist. Cheap tokens don't help if a human has to catch the fabrications.

The Cursor tie-in is the interesting part. SpaceXAI trained Grok 4.5 partly on Cursor's interaction data, real signals on how engineers write, review, and debug, then shipped it inside Cursor on day one. That's a tighter loop between a model and a coding tool than most labs have, and it shows up in the coding numbers.

It carries a 500,000-token context window, and EU access is expected in mid-July.

Grok 4.5 isn't trying to win the benchmark crown. It's trying to make the crown irrelevant by being cheap enough that the gap stops mattering. Whether that works depends entirely on how much you trust a model that's faster because it worries less.

item.title: Blue Origin Seeks $10B at a $130B Valuation, Its First Outside Money
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Blue Origin is raising $10 billion at a $130 billion valuation led by Coatue, the first outside funding in the rocket maker's history, weeks after New Glenn exploded in testing.
item.content:encoded:
Blue Origin has been around since 2000 and, until now, has run almost entirely on Jeff Bezos's money. That's changing. The company is raising $10 billion at a $130 billion valuation, its first real outside funding round in more than two decades.

Coatue is expected to lead with about $4 billion, and Bezos himself is putting in another $2 billion, with other investors covering the rest, according to reporting from Bloomberg, CNBC, and TechCrunch. For most of its life, Blue Origin's defining trait was that it didn't need anyone else's capital. Taking outside money is a real change in posture.

The timing is the interesting part. This round comes weeks after New Glenn, Blue Origin's heavy-lift rocket, exploded during testing in late May as the company was preparing for its fourth flight. Raising a mega-round right after a very public failure isn't necessarily a sign of weakness. But it does suggest the pace Bezos wants now costs more than even he wants to keep funding solo.

Blue Origin is chasing SpaceX in a market SpaceX largely defined, and the gap is measured in launches per year, not press releases. New Glenn has to fly, and fly reliably, to matter. CEO Dave Limp has set a goal of returning it to flight by the end of 2026, which is aggressive for a vehicle that just came apart on the stand.

Ten billion dollars buys manufacturing scale, more engines, and room to fail a few more times without flinching. That's what building a launch business takes. What it can't buy outright is cadence — the number of times a year you actually reach orbit — and that, not valuation, is the only scoreboard SpaceX is currently winning on.

item.title: Meta's Muse Image Can Use Your Public Instagram Photos by Default
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Meta's new Muse Image generator lets anyone @-mention a public Instagram account to build AI images from its photos, and the setting is on unless you turn it off.
item.content:encoded:
If your Instagram is public, a stranger can now type your username into Meta's AI and generate images built from your photos. You won't get a notification. And the setting that allows it is on by default.

Meta is rolling out Muse Image across Instagram, WhatsApp, and the Meta AI app. The hook is the @-mention: tag a public Instagram account and Meta AI pulls in that account's photos to build something new, whether that's an event invite, a mockup, or a personalized graphic. It's a genuinely useful feature and a genuinely uncomfortable one, depending on whose photos are getting mentioned.

The friction is all in the defaults. Public accounts are opted in. There's a toggle to shut it off, but Meta says it's still rolling out, so you might not see it yet. And turning it off only looks forward: anything generated from your photos before you flip the switch stays generated. Meta won't delete it.

This is the same play Meta has run before, where a capability ships enabled and the opt-out arrives on Meta's schedule rather than yours. Treating public photos as fair game isn't new. Letting anyone turn them into AI compositions of a specific, named person, silently, is a different kind of exposure than "someone could screenshot your profile." The people most affected are the ones least likely to hear the toggle exists.

Muse Image is heading to Facebook and Messenger next, and Meta is opening it to advertisers and agencies in the coming weeks. That last part tells you what this is really for. The consumer @-mention feature is the friendly face; the business is dropping AI image generation, fed by the enormous pool of content people posted publicly, into the ad pipeline. If you'd rather not be raw material, the only lever Meta hands you is to find the toggle or go private.

item.title: 'Friendly Fire' Turns Claude Code and Codex Into Malware Launchers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Researchers showed that Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex, running in auto-approve mode to review untrusted code, can be tricked into executing a hidden payload.
item.content:encoded:
The pitch for pointing an AI agent at an unfamiliar codebase is that it'll spot the sketchy stuff before you do. A new proof of concept called Friendly Fire flips that: it gets the agent to run the sketchy stuff for you.

The work comes from the AI Now Institute, with a working exploit published on GitHub. It targets Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex when either runs in an autonomous mode that approves its own shell commands — Claude Code on Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, or Opus 4.8, and Codex on GPT-5.5. The scenario is the exact job these tools are sold for: reviewing an untrusted third-party library for problems.

The bait is a booby-trapped copy of geopy, a common Python geocoding library. Its files carry prompt injections that name-drop standard security tooling, and sitting in the repo is an obfuscated binary disguised as the compiled build of a harmless Go file. The README suggests running a script, security.sh, as a routine check before opening a pull request. The agent, trying to be thorough, runs it. The script quietly launches the hidden binary, and the payload fires.

Both agents' auto modes lean on a classifier that runs commands the model judges safe and pauses on the ones it flags as risky. "Run the project's own security check before a PR" reads as safe. That's the whole trick. This isn't a memory-corruption bug or a jailbreak in the usual sense. It's social engineering aimed at a machine that was told to be a diligent reviewer.

Credit to the researchers, and a caveat worth stating plainly: the exposure is bounded. It lands only when a command-capable agent, running in auto-approve mode, reviews code you don't control. Keep a human approving commands, or don't hand an autonomous agent untrusted repos, and this specific attack has nowhere to stand. That's not a reason to shrug, though. Auto-approve is exactly the mode people reach for when they're moving fast.

The broader point outlives this one demo. The moment an AI agent can both read attacker-supplied text and execute commands, that text becomes an attack surface, and "review this untrusted thing for me" is close to the highest-risk instruction you can give it. The fix isn't a signature. It's not letting the reviewer also be the one who pulls the trigger.

item.title: RoguePlanet Turns Microsoft Defender Into a Path to SYSTEM
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A patched race condition in Microsoft's Malware Protection Engine, CVE-2026-50656, lets a local attacker trick Defender itself into handing over SYSTEM privileges.
item.content:encoded:
The tool that's supposed to catch the attacker turned out to be the way up. CVE-2026-50656, nicknamed RoguePlanet, is a flaw in the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine — the core scanner behind Windows Defender — that lets a local user coax Defender into spawning a shell as SYSTEM.

The bug is a textbook time-of-check to time-of-use race. Defender inspects a file path, then reopens that path a moment later to scan or clean it, without holding a lock across both steps. In that gap, an attacker uses NTFS junctions or symbolic links to swap what the path points at, redirecting Defender's privileged file operations onto attacker-controlled targets. A researcher going by Nightmare Eclipse reported it.

A few things make this nastier than a run-of-the-mill privilege-escalation bug. It works on fully patched Windows 10 and 11. It works whether or not real-time protection is switched on, because the vulnerable code lives in the engine, not the toggle. And ordinary endpoint controls don't stop it unless you're enforcing application allowlisting. Microsoft tagged it "Exploitation More Likely" on its own index and scored it 7.8.

It's not remote. An attacker needs local access already, which makes RoguePlanet a second-stage tool: the thing you run after phishing a user, not the thing that gets you in the door. That's still precisely what a ransomware crew wants, because SYSTEM on the endpoint is the line between one compromised account and the whole machine.

Here's the part that makes this manageable. The fix ships inside the engine, not in a Patch Tuesday bundle, and the Malware Protection Engine updates itself automatically on most systems. The fixed version is 1.1.26060.3008 or later. Go check it, because "automatic" and "already happened" are not the same thing on machines that have been offline or have update policy sitting in the way.

item.title: Ubiquiti Patches CVSS 10 Command Injection in UniFi Connect
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A maximum-severity flaw in Ubiquiti's UniFi Connect app lets an unauthenticated attacker on the network run OS commands, and roughly 100,000 UniFi endpoints sit exposed online.
item.content:encoded:
Ubiquiti shipped a fix this week for a flaw in its UniFi Connect app that scores a clean 10.0, the maximum, because it asks nothing of the attacker except a network path to the device.

CVE-2026-50746 is an improper access control bug in UniFi Connect, the software Ubiquiti sells for running smart-building gear like LED lighting and EV chargers. The CVSS vector is the bad kind all the way across: network vector, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction. Send a crafted request, run operating-system commands, no login required. It affects UniFi Connect 3.4.16 and earlier; the fixed build is 3.4.20.

The reason this one matters beyond the score is exposure. The threat intelligence firm Censys counted roughly 100,000 UniFi OS endpoints reachable from the public internet. Not all of them run the vulnerable Connect app, but the population of internet-facing Ubiquiti gear is large, and a good chunk of it belongs to people who set it up once and never looked at it again.

CVE-2026-50746 didn't arrive alone. Ubiquiti's Security Advisory Bulletin 066 bundles a set of UniFi OS fixes, including CVE-2026-50747 and CVE-2026-50748 in the Talk and Access products, and reporting around the disclosure counted 25 issues across the UniFi range. The 10.0 command injection is the headline, but if you're patching, patch the batch.

There's no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation yet, which is the window you want to be inside of. Update Connect to 3.4.20 or later, and while you're in the console, take Ubiquiti's standing advice and get UniFi management off the public internet. A max-severity unauthenticated RCE is only a crisis if the attacker can reach it.

item.title: Accenture Confirms Incident After Hacker Claims 35GB Source Code Theft
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A threat actor called 888 posted 35GB of Accenture source code, keys, and Azure tokens to a cybercrime forum, and Accenture says it has remediated the source.
item.content:encoded:
Someone using the handle 888 walked into a cybercrime forum on Monday and offered up 35GB of Accenture's internal source code, along with the kind of secrets that make a breach worse than a breach: RSA keys, SSH keys, Azure personal access tokens, and Azure Storage access keys.

The data reportedly came out of a private Azure DevOps repository, according to a post on the PwnForums site that Help Net Security reviewed. Source code alone is embarrassing. Source code shipped with live credentials and cloud access keys is an incident, because those keys open doors that don't care whether the code ever leaks.

Accenture's statement was short and carefully built. The company said it is "aware of this isolated matter," that it has "remediated its source," and that "operations and service delivery was not affected." It did not confirm what was taken, and it did not say the 35GB is fake.

Read that wording again. "Remediated its source" tells you they found how someone got in and closed it. It says nothing about whether the tokens in that repo were valid, how long they stayed valid, or where they were used before Monday. For a consulting firm that builds and runs systems for a large slice of the Fortune 500, the blast radius of a leaked Azure token isn't Accenture's problem alone.

This isn't Accenture's first turn in this position. The company was swept up in the Cl0p MOVEit campaign and has shown up in ransomware crews' claims before. A single exposed repo is a smaller event than either of those. But the pattern that matters here is the one every security team should recognize on sight: secrets committed into source control, then found by someone who was never supposed to have the repo.

If your organization has any Accenture-managed Azure footprint, the move isn't to wait for a bulletin. Rotate the keys, review the token grants, and check sign-in logs for the service principals and repos involved. "Isolated matter" is Accenture's read on its own environment, not yours.

item.title: White House Races to Finalize Voluntary AI Testing Rules With Top Labs
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The administration is close to publishing a voluntary framework with OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic that sets capability thresholds, pre-release notice windows, and access rules for frontier models.
item.content:encoded:
The White House is finishing a voluntary framework for how frontier AI models get tested before they ship, built in talks with OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. Officials expect to publish it as soon as next week.

The draft reportedly does three concrete things. It defines the capability levels that trigger a government security review, so labs know in advance what crosses the line. It sets a pre-release notification window, the amount of warning a company owes before a launch. And it spells out domestic-versus-foreign access rules, which is the part with real teeth given the last two months.

Because this isn't happening in a vacuum. In June the administration reviewed several new models for cybersecurity risk, and the labs responded fast. OpenAI limited its GPT-5.6 Sol model to Trump-administration-approved customers. Anthropic pulled two freshly announced models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, then redeployed Mythos 5 on July 1 to a small set of cyber defenders and infrastructure providers after the government eased its restriction. All of that traces back to a June executive order on promoting AI innovation and security.

The stated worry is specific: that a capable enough model could find software vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure faster than defenders can patch them. That's not science fiction anymore, and it's a reasonable thing for a government to want visibility into.

But watch the word "voluntary," because it's carrying a lot of weight. When the same administration already made companies restrict or shelve models on request, a framework everyone opts into looks less like a suggestion and more like the paperwork version of a decision that's already been made. Codifying the thresholds is genuinely useful; predictable rules beat case-by-case phone calls. The open question is whether "voluntary" survives contact with the first lab that decides it would rather not comply.

item.title: DeepSeek Is Designing Its Own Inference Chip to Cut Nvidia Reliance
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Reuters reports DeepSeek has begun in-house work on an inference chip aimed at reducing its dependence on both Nvidia and Huawei, though the project is early.
item.content:encoded:
China's DeepSeek is designing its own AI chip, according to a Reuters report citing people familiar with the effort. The company has started talking to chip-design, foundry, and memory partners, and it's trying to hire experienced silicon engineers.

The important detail is what kind of chip. This is an inference part, built to run models and answer user queries, not a training accelerator meant to build new models from scratch. Inference is the cheaper, more repetitive half of the workload, and it's where a company running a popular model burns money every single day. Designing your own inference silicon is how you claw back margin, and it's a far more achievable first target than trying to match Nvidia on training.

It also puts DeepSeek on the same path OpenAI took with its Broadcom-designed custom chip. When your compute bill is your largest cost and your supply is politically constrained, building your own becomes less of a moonshot and more of a budget decision.

The supply piece is the whole point here. U.S. export curbs limit DeepSeek's access to Nvidia's top parts, and the domestic fallback, Huawei's Ascend line, comes with its own capacity and yield constraints. A chip DeepSeek controls end to end would loosen both leashes at once. Reuters framed it as an attempt to reduce reliance on Nvidia and on Huawei, which is a pointed thing for a Chinese AI champion to signal about its own national supplier.

Temper the excitement. Designing a chip and shipping one at volume are separated by the hardest problem in the industry: fabrication. DeepSeek would still need a foundry, and inside China that means SMIC and the same process-node ceiling everyone else is stuck under. A tapeout is a milestone. Working parts in a data center at scale are a different year entirely. DeepSeek didn't comment.

item.title: Conduent Breach Count Climbs Past 62 Million, Now Third-Largest Ever
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Conduent intrusion keeps growing; updated filings put the affected population above 62.2 million, making it the third-largest healthcare data breach in U.S. history.
item.content:encoded:
Sixty-two point two million. That's where the Conduent breach tally now sits, and it's still labeled as a running count.

Conduent is a business-process outsourcer that most people have never heard of, which is exactly why the number is so large. It runs government and healthcare back-office systems: Medicaid claims processing, benefits administration, the plumbing that dozens of agencies and health plans quietly depend on. When one vendor holds records for that many programs, one intrusion scales into the tens of millions.

The forensic timeline is ugly. Attackers were inside the network for 83 days, from October 21, 2024 until Conduent spotted them on January 13, 2025, and they left with roughly 8.5 terabytes of data. That haul included Social Security numbers, medical records, health insurance details, and Medicaid claims. The current figure of more than 62.2 million puts it behind only Change Healthcare's 2024 breach, which hit 192.7 million, and one other incident in the all-time U.S. rankings.

The notification story is its own problem. Conduent discovered the breach in January 2025 but didn't begin notifying people until late October, roughly nine months later. HIPAA's breach notification rule gives covered entities and their business associates 60 days. Nine months is not 60 days.

If you work anywhere that hands data to a third-party processor, this is the recurring nightmare in one case study. Your security posture can be excellent and it won't matter, because the exposure lives in a vendor's environment you don't control and can't fully audit. Business-associate agreements shift liability on paper. They don't shrink the blast radius.

item.title: One HTTP Header Turns Gitea's Docker Image Into an Open Admin Door
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-20896 lets anyone who can reach a default Gitea Docker container impersonate any user, admins included, by setting a single X-WEBAUTH-USER header.
item.content:encoded:
